sentences.text: The type species Gavialosuchus eggenburgensis is known from fossils found in the early Miocene of Austria.
Recent molecular studies indicate that tomistomines, including Gavialosuchus, belong to Gavialoidea rather than being crocodiles.
A specimen of G. americanus is estimated to have reached 9.75 meters based on a skull measuring 132 centimeters.
Unlike modern freshwater relatives, Gavialosuchus was an estuarine and coastal crocodilian living in shallow marine waters.
The genus Gavialosuchus was described by Toula and Kail in 1885.
Two other species, G. americanus and G. carolinensis, have been reclassified into other genera.
A 2012 study by Brochu and Storrs found strong support for the suggestion that G. americanus and G. carolinensis belong to the genus Thecachampsa, a view agreed upon by a 2018 study by Weems.
Gavialosuchus lived in Europe during the early Miocene and in eastern North America during the late Oligocene and Miocene.
The time range for Gavialosuchus is from the Chattian to the Tortonian, between 27.3 and 7.246 million years ago.
The classification of Gavialosuchus remains an unresolved issue.
